extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian aesthetics and teleology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for judging purposiveness and natural purpose (teleology) from the Analytic of the Teleological Judgement; aimed at interpreting how to classify objects/events as purposive or as natural purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective purposiveness — formal vs material
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish objective purposiveness that is merely formal (intellectual purposiveness of concepts/figures) from material/objective purposiveness (purposiveness in things themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal objective purposiveness: e.g., geometrical figures (circle, conic sections) display purposiveness for many problems by virtue of intellectual construction; this is an objective intellectual satisfaction but is 'merely formal' because it does not make the concept of the object possible by itself and does not imply an actual external purpose. Material/objective purposiveness requires the order/regularity to be empirically present in things (e.g., a garden) and thus depends on a concept of a purpose grounded in the object's existence. Note: call formal purposiveness 'relative perfection' rather than beauty; demonstrations invoking concepts strengthen Understanding and Imagination (are 'elegant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative purposiveness vs inner purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish relative purposiveness (utility or mere advantage as means for other beings) from inner purposiveness (a purpose intrinsic to the natural being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative purposiveness: examples include rivers depositing earth useful for plants, sandy soils favoring pines, snow protecting crops — these are advantageous relations but do not by themselves justify judging them as ends of nature. Inner purposiveness: when a thing is to be judged as a purpose of nature itself (not merely useful to others). Relative purposiveness can hint at natural purposes but 'justifies no absolute teleological judgement.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for regarding an object as a natural purpose (contingency of form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thing is forced to be considered a purpose (rather than a mere mechanical product) when its form is not possible according to mere natural laws and when empirical knowledge of it presupposes concepts of Reason; i.e., its form is contingently intelligible without mechanistic explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If chance/mechanical causes cannot plausibly account for a given regularity or form (e.g., finding a precise geometric figure in nature), we are inclined to attribute its genesis to Reason or design. However, to be a natural purpose (not an artifact), additional criteria (see self-causation/organised being) are required. The distinction between 'product of art' and 'natural purpose' hinges on whether causality must be traced to an external rational agent or can be attributed regulatively to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural purposes must be (in a double sense) cause and effect of themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: To regard something as a natural purpose requires that it be both cause and effect of itself—generative and formative—so that its particular form cannot be fully explained by external mechanical causes alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) A tree reproduces generically (produces same genus); (2) A tree produces itself individually via growth using material it transforms; (3) Parts of a tree reciprocally generate and support one another (buds, leaves, twigs). This self-referential causality (reciprocal generation/maintenance) grounds the judgement of natural purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings as necessary bearers of natural purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Only organised beings (organisms) can be judged as possible only as purposes of nature; organisation is the hallmark of natural purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organised beings display internal formative power: their parts not only move but have formative, self-propagating capacities that organise incoming matter into functional parts. Unlike a watch (machine) whose parts are instruments but do not produce one another, organised beings produce and repair their parts, replace missing parts, and show reciprocal dependence among parts. Thus, organisation (self-organisation, internal formative power) is the criterion distinguishing natural purposes from mere machines or artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle/definition of internal purposiveness in organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose and means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim functions as an a priori regulative principle for judging internal purposiveness: in an organism nothing is vain or merely chance; parts exist for the sake of the whole and for one another (each part is both end and instrument). Practitioners (e.g., anatomists) adopt this as a fundamental guiding proposition for investigation. It is not a constitutive law of nature but a necessary regulative maxim for inquiry into organised beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity of parts as cause and effect (systemic unity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For teleological judgement, the parts of a natural product must be such that each part's being and form is possible only through reference to the whole, and parts reciprocally determine one another (mutual cause-effect in form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demands that the unity of the whole be the ground for the form and combination of parts (the Idea of the whole determines what must be contained in it). If parts can be explained purely as mechanical concretions independent of the whole, teleological judgement is less justified. The reciprocity enables judging an effective-cause series as an effect through final causes (systematic unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as regulative (not constitutive) principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological concepts (purposes of nature) are not constitutive concepts that establish factual causality; they serve as regulative analogies guiding reflection and investigation into natural phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We may use teleological judgement analogically (by comparison with our purposive causality) to bring phenomena under principles for observation and inquiry where mechanical causality alone is insufficient, but we must not claim teleology as an explanatory constitutive principle that introduces a new kind of causality into natural science. Calling nature an 'analogon of art' can mislead; teleology is a heuristic/regulative device to direct investigation and admiration, not an ontological claim that nature is produced by an external rational agent.
